title: Add territory-aware RBACv2 + audit-velocity controls and KMS fencing middleware
author: Aisha Kapoor
release_notes: Adds territory-aware RBACv2 enforcement, a lightweight KMS "fencing" middleware for region-bound key selection, and an "audit velocity" signal used by alerts to detect anomalous policy churn. Backwards compatible: existing policies continue to work; new territory fields are optional.
description: Context and motivation: several enterprise customers requested tighter enforcement of regional residency policies while preserving operator ergonomics. This PR implements a territory-aware extension to RBACv2, a KMS fencing middleware that prefers region-anchored CMKs and provides a safe fallback, and an audit-velocity metric that surfaces policy mutation bursts for SOC teams. Design summary: 1) RBACv2 schema gains an optional 'territory' clause that can be attached to role bindings and service-account templates. 2) A decision-cache layer was extended to include territory-matching logic to minimize latency impact on authz checks. 3) The KMS fencing middleware inspects the resolved territory and attempts to use a region-scoped CMK path; if unavailable, it records an auditable refusal or a policy-driven fallback (configurable per tenant). 4) Audit-velocity computes a per-tenant rolling window of policy mutation rate and emits an alert label when thresholds are exceeded. Checklist: - [x] API/DB schema changes for territory metadata and index - [x] Decision cache territory-aware lookup and TTL heuristics - [x] KMS middleware with safe fallback and metrics (kms.fence_attempts, kms.fence_fallbacks) - [x] Audit-velocity producer and alert labels - [x] Unit & integration tests for decision matrix and crypto fallback - [x] Migration script to backfill empty territory -> 'global' for existing tenants - [x] Canary rollout config and feature flag (rbac.territory_v1) - [x] Docs and console labels for territory on role pages Implementation notes: territory matching is implemented as a three-tier comparison (explicit tenant territory, service-level override, default/global). To avoid performance regressions the decision-cache now stores a compact territory fingerprint and a short TTL for changeable bindings. KMS fencing uses an injected KMS resolver that attempts 'tenant://{tenant_id}/cmk/{zone}' then falls back to global CMK with audit reason recorded. The default behavior is 'audit-and-fallback' behind the feature flag; customers can opt-in to 'strict-refuse' per tenant via the admin API. Migration and rollout: we backfilled territories as 'global' in a migration to ensure deterministic behavior. The rollout used a canary group (5% of accounts) for 72 hours; we monitored latency, authorization failure rates, kms.fallback ratio, and audit-velocity alerts. Observability: New metrics emitted: rbac.territory_miss, rbac.territory_match_latency_ms, kms.fence_attempts_total, kms.fence_fallback_total, audit.velocity.window_1h. Logs include structured reason codes for fallback decisions to help post-mortems. Backwards compatibility: existing role bindings without territory continue to match all territories. Security review notes: the KMS resolver operates with least privilege and never exposes key material; unit tests include simulated KMS outages to validate fallback logic and audit entries. Related work: builds on ENG-1089 decision cache refactor and reuses parts of the operator-scoped constraint code. Linear/Jira references included above.
